I'm Nandini. I've shared a flat with Sonali for two years, and the month after her father's surgery she changed in ways I noticed but didn't fully understand.
She stopped watching shows with me. I'd find her on the balcony at eleven with a notebook, not writing much. Once she asked me, out of nowhere, whether I thought people in a hundred years would know we'd existed. I said probably not, and she nodded as if that was the answer she expected and didn't like.
I asked if she was okay. She said she wasn't sad exactly, just thinking about how short everything is. She said she'd talked to her cousin, and was going to see the counsellor at work. She did go.
By the end of the month she'd signed up to teach Saturday classes at the shelter near the market. She came back from the first one talking fast, hands moving.

qa.a: She found her on the balcony with a notebook.

qa.a: She seemed unsettled and heavy with thoughts about how short life is, uneasy rather than simply sad.

After the funeral: Nazia, twenty-five, drove back from her cousin Bilal's funeral on a Thursday and couldn't sleep. He had been twenty-eight. At 2 a.m. she opened her work laptop, looked at a spreadsheet of shipping schedules and thought: is this what my one life is for?
Four days later: On an evening walk, she told her friend Vishal. “I'm not in danger or anything. I'm just scared of wasting it.”
Vishal listened, then said, “Scared how? What would not wasting it look like?”
She didn't know. That annoyed her.
Two weeks later: She sat with a notebook and wrote three questions: Who do I want near me? What do I want to have made? What do I want to have fixed? She didn't answer them all. But she emailed the literacy centre near her office and asked about weekend tutoring. Some nights were still hard. Fewer.

qa.q: How old was Nazia's cousin Bilal?
qa.a: He had been twenty-eight.

qa.q: What was Nazia afraid of after the funeral?
qa.a: She felt scared of wasting her one life, a dread about meaning rather than any danger to herself.

qa.q: Why was Vishal's question helpful?
qa.a: Asking what not wasting it would look like turned a vague dread into something Nazia could start to think through.

qa.q: What would change if Nazia had kept the fear to herself?
qa.a: She might have stayed stuck in sleepless worry without the push to name what she wanted and take a small step.

grounding: Over weeks a young woman grapples with mortality after a death and begins to shape a sense of purpose.

Dhruv, you asked if I was ever afraid of dying. Come, sit. Your Sharmila Nani will tell you.
I was twenty-five when my mother fell ill for the last time. I nursed her for eight months. At night, after she slept, I lay awake counting my own heartbeats. If she could go, so could I. So could everyone. What was any of it for?
One night she woke and saw my face. She didn't lecture me. She held my hand and asked me to read her the letters my father had written before they married. I read until dawn.
After she died, I kept thinking about those letters. Somebody had cared enough to write them, and somebody had kept them fifty years. That was an answer, of a kind.
I started writing too, to my sisters, to your mother. I still get afraid, Dhruv. But now I know what I'm doing while I'm here.

At 6:30 every evening, Rajni unlocked the small room above the ration shop in a Kolkata lane and laid out slates for eleven women.
She was twenty-six. Three years ago she had quit a well-paid office job to run this reading class, and most weeks felt like pushing a cart uphill. Women missed class for work, for sick children, for husbands who didn't like it.
On Tuesday, Chandrika, a fifty-year-old who cooked in four houses, was late. She came in breathless, holding her phone up.
“Didi! On the bus. I read the board. Shyambazar. I read it myself and got down at the right stop.”
The other women clapped. Chandrika sat down, embarrassed and beaming.
Rajni turned to the blackboard so nobody would see her eyes fill. Three years of pushing the cart. It was enough, this. It was enough for a long while.

“Alka, it's been four years in that village. When are you coming back to Nagpur?”
“Maa, I'm not unhappy here.”
“You're an engineer. Your classmates are in Bengaluru, in big companies.”
“And I'm here building check dams with farmers who've never had water after March.” Alka sat on the steps of the site office, phone to her ear. “Today the Bhoyar family got their first summer crop in eleven years. The old man made me eat jaggery from his own hand.”
Vandana sighed. “You sound tired.”
“I am tired. I'm also… I don't know the word. Full? Like I'm where I'm supposed to be.”
“And later? Marriage? A house?”
“Later, Maa. I'll plan for those too. But I want them built around this, not instead of it.”
A long pause. “Send me a photo of the dam,” Vandana said, softer.

Aditi, people think a school counsellor must go home crying every night. In my first year, I did. I'm Binita, and I was twenty-four and I took every child's story home in my chest.
A boy whose parents were divorcing. A girl who hadn't eaten lunch because of teasing. I would lie awake replaying their faces.
My supervisor, Mrs D'Costa, finally sat me down. She said, “You have to feel it with them in the room, and then you have to leave it in the room. Otherwise you'll be no use to them by March.”
So I made a small ritual. At four, I write my notes, close the file and wash my hands at the staff sink, slowly. Then I walk home the long way.
I still understand them, maybe better now. I just don't carry them. They need me steady more than they need me sad.

I'm Devika. I sit next to Yusuf at the airline helpdesk, and last Sunday a man shouted at him for eleven minutes.
His flight to Dubai had been cancelled and he'd miss his brother's wedding. He called Yusuf useless, then worse. I could hear him through Yusuf's headset.
Yusuf didn't argue. He said, “I understand you'll miss your brother's wedding. That's awful. Let me see what's possible.” His voice stayed low and even. He found a seat on a different airline, leaving four hours later. The man went quiet, then said, “Sorry. It's not you.”
When the call ended, Yusuf took his headset off, closed his eyes for three breaths and drank some water. Then he put the headset back on.
I asked if he was okay. He said, “He was scared, not angry at me.” I don't know how he manages that.

“It hurt,” she said. “A lot.”

The month I got my first real salary, at twenty-four, I wanted a new phone and a trip to Goa. My mother, Neelam, wanted something else: a meeting with a certified financial planner, a woman from her office who does this properly.
I sulked in the car. I'm Kashish, and I thought it would be boring.
It wasn't. She asked what I'd want in five, ten and twenty years. Would I support Mummy one day? Did I have health insurance of my own? I didn't. She explained the options without pushing any product, and told me to read every document and ask questions before signing.
We didn't decide everything that day. I took the papers home and read them twice. I still went to Goa, later, with money I'd set aside.
Mostly I remember that my mother had never had anyone explain these things to her. She sat very still, listening.

qa.a: She sat very still, listening, perhaps moved to learn things nobody had ever explained to her.

The letter offering Nitin the Singapore post sat on the dining table in their Chennai flat for three days.
He was twenty-six, an engineer with a water company, and the post was a big step. It also meant leaving the flood-response project he had built in the city's poorest wards over two monsoons.
His wife Rehana didn't tell him what to do. On the third night she asked, “When you're fifty, what do you want to have been part of?”
He thought about the woman in Velachery who had brought him tea after her street stayed dry for the first time. He thought about the children they wanted, and where they would grow up.
On Friday he wrote back declining the post, and asked his manager for a role that would let him expand the project to two more districts. Rehana put the letter in a folder, not the bin. “Just in case,” she said.

qa.a: He felt torn between a career step and a project he cared about deeply.

qa.a: It helped Nitin look at the long-term shape of his life, not just the next job.

qa.a: She seems supportive but practical, backing his choice while keeping the letter just in case.

grounding: A young engineer shapes career and family plans around long-term service to his city.

The sand company's offer came to the panchayat office in Malpur during the harvest season, and Gargi, twenty-six and the village's youngest sarpanch, had a week to answer.
The money would pay for a new school roof. But the river bank near the fields was already crumbling, and the company wanted to dig there.
